title: W.L. Jackson, his Chicago trumpet teacher
summary: Blakeney describes teacher W.L. Jackson, a talker and violinist who raised Erskine and Charles Tate and told him to join the union.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Mr. Blakeney, was that your first music teacher?
Yes it was--no, not my first, because I told you I took piano lessons in Mississippi.
My aunt gave me piano lessons in Mississippi.
Maybe you'd like to tell us just a little bit about him.
W.L. Jackson was a great talker. He used to claim to be one of the best violinists in the country, and after I had my lesson every night he would sit down and just talk about his experiences.
He would talk about how he
raised Erskine and his brother Charles. His brother Charles played trumpet, and Erskine played violin, and how he used to take him to recitals and how good they were and he would brag about them.

When they moved to Chicago, he separated from their mother. He wasn't the father of these kids, he was just the step-father; he married their mother. She had her own music school and he had his own music school.

W.L. Jackson, I kind of liked him because I liked the way he talked;and then after I was with him three years, he said I think you're good enough now, you ought to go down to the union and kind of work yourself in with the professionals. Of course instead of doing that I did it differently, I went with the band and started out that way.
